Retry yields only marginal reduction (40.9\% vs.\ baseline 42.9\%, ${\sim}$2~pp across three trials; Fisher exact $p > 0.6$). $10{\times}$ capability scaling reduces death rate to ${\sim}$35\% ($\Delta \approx -17$~pp). That two independent mechanisms (parameter scaling and verbal self-correction) converge to nearly identical death-rate floors suggests a shared bound set by the internal strategy's lack of ground-truth state access, not by any single intervention's limitations. Compounding state estimation errors across multi-step trajectories create catastrophic failures that single-axis improvements attenuate but do not eliminate. Tree search with environment feedback and frontier models remain untested. Prior tool-routing work \citep{toolformer-2023,art-2023,chameleon-2023} operates in non-interactive settings where individual tool calls are independent; in multi-step interactive environments, the finding is not that death exists but that the death-rate differential ($\delta = 26.6$~pp) and its downstream effects resist all three tested intervention axes.

All 73 internal-strategy deaths trace to a single action pattern: \texttt{focus on [object]}. In ScienceWorld, \texttt{focus on} is the answer-submission action; the LLM systematically misuses it as a general interaction command, applying it to irrelevant targets (rooms, doors, inventory items) and thereby submitting incorrect answers that trigger the $-100$ penalty. The root cause is thus action-space grounding failure, not comprehension failure: 78.1\% of dying agents demonstrate task understanding, yet 97.3\% fail to translate it into correct actions. Among fatal targets, \texttt{workshop} alone accounts for 44.6\%, indicating a systematic object bias rather than random exploration (Figure~\ref{fig:death-action-dist}). This specificity suggests that targeted interventions (action-space filtering, grounding-aware prompting) could reduce death rates more effectively than general capability scaling.

Cross-environment contrasts confirm framework predictions: on MATH ($N{=}795$), no routing signal emerges without catastrophic failure ($p = 0.81$).
